desc:
A binary tree is height-balanced if, for every node, the heights of its left and right subtrees differ by at most one (the height of the empty tree is 0). Count the structurally different height-balanced binary search trees that store exactly the values 1, 2, ..., n.

Two trees are different if their shapes differ. Return the count modulo 1,000,000,007.

Example 1

n = 4
Output: 4
The root has subtrees of 2 and 1 nodes, or 1 and 2 nodes; the 2-node subtree can lean left or right: 2 × 2 = 4 shapes.

Example 2

n = 3
Output: 1
hints: A balanced tree with n nodes has height only about log n. That limits how many different heights you ever have to consider.
For a root whose subtrees have heights a and b, balance requires |a - b| ≤ 1, and the whole tree has height 1 + max(a, b). So you need counts of balanced trees by (number of nodes, exact height).

Let g[k][d] be the number of balanced shapes with k nodes and height exactly d. For the root with i nodes on the left and k-1-i on the right: combine g[i][d-1] * g[j][d-1], g[i][d-1] * g[j][d-2] and g[i][d-2] * g[j][d-1]. Only heights up to about 1.44 log2 n occur.
editorial: State: g[k][d] = number of height-balanced shapes with k nodes and height exactly d, with g[0][0] = 1. For a tree of height d the subtree heights are (d-1, d-1), (d-1, d-2) or (d-2, d-1); all other pairs are either unbalanced or give a different total height. With a left subtree of i nodes and a right subtree of j = k-1-i nodes, add the products of the matching counts for these three cases.

The smallest balanced tree of height d has N(d) = 1 + N(d-1) + N(d-2) nodes (Fibonacci-like, N(1) = 1, N(2) = 2) and the largest has 2d-1 nodes, so d never exceeds roughly 1.44 log2(n+2) and each k only has a couple of feasible heights. The cost is O(n² log n) time and O(n log n) space. The answer is the sum of g[n][d] over all d. The sequence starts 1, 2, 1, 4, 6, 4, 17, 32, ...
